Prof Dr Nazia Mumtaz
PhD

Riphah International University,

DEFINITION
Human development is the scientific study of processes of change & stability.
Process of growing to maturity.  
Study of a human life-cycle from conception to death.
In biological terms, this entails growth from a one-celled zygote to an adult human being.

GROWTH
Growth is quantitative
Growth comprises of height, weight, size & shape of body organs
Cell  division
Growth is for limited period

DEVELOPMENT
Development is qualitative as well as quantitative 
In this with physical changes, cognitive, social & emotional change also included
Due to motor development & adjust mental processes & their interplay
Development takes place till death
 It can be observed by matured behavior

Growth & Development
Growth
Implies  physical change, usually resulting from either an increase in cell number or cell size
Development:
A change or modification in a person’s capacity to function; enhancement of a skill

BALTES’s LIFE SPAN DEVELOPMENT
Paul B. Baltes & Colleagues Identified Six Key Principles of Life Span Development
Development is life long
Development involve both gain & loss
Relative influence of biology & culture shift over  life span
Development involves a changing allocation of resources
Development is modifiable
Development is influenced by historical and cultural context

CHILD DEVELOPMENT
INTRODUCTION 
Child development is  multifaceted, integral, & continual process of change in which children become able to handle ever more complex levels of moving, thinking, feeling, & relating to others.

Cont..
Child development is a gradual unfolding of biologically determined characteristics & traits that arises as child learns from experiences 
The first 1000 days of life span from day of conception till  child attends two years of age (UNICEF), is consider most important development phase.


https://www.unicef.org/laos/ensuring-healthy-start-first-1000-days-0

Cont…
Globally, more than 200 million children under five years fail to reach their potential in cognitive & social development due to poverty, poor health, malnutrition & deficit care
Most of which is borne by developing countries
Most of these children live in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, are exposed to multiple risks including poverty, malnutrition, poor health & un-stimulating home environment, while detrimentally affecting their development.

Cont…
Other factors that compromise overall development during pregnancy & after birth are parent’s behavioral, dietary deficiencies, chronic infections, exclusive breastfeeding, inadequate feeding practices & lack of stimulation
Over 43% of children under the age of 5 are at risk of not fulfilling their full developmental potential as per   UNICEF in 2017

CHILD DEVELOPMENT
Child development refers to  biological & psychological changes that occur in human beings between birth & end of adolescence
Individual  progresses from dependency to increasing autonomy
Gradual  change  occurs as  central nervous system matures & shows psychological reactions

Cont…
INFLUENCED BY
Genetic factors in  prenatal period
Biologic influences in  prenatal & post natal period & in early years of life
Environmental factors

CHILD DEVELOPMENT
DEVELOPING BRAIN
At birth , brain has 100 billion neurons
Each neuron --- 15,000 synapses by 3 yrs of age
Number of synapses remain constant but number of neurons decreases gradually
Used pathways - preserved , & less used ones atrophy

Cont..
      The brain requires multiple inputs: 

Stimulation & care to spark neural connections across multiple regions of  brain to increase its capacity & function
Access to good quality early childhood education programs that provide children with early cognitive & language skills, build social competency & support emotional development 
Adequate health & nutrition at right time to feed & nourish the architecture of body, including brain, during sensitive periods of development required

Cont..
      The brain requires multiple inputs: 
It requires safety & protection to buffer against stress and allow absorption of nutrients with growth & development of  nervous system - including the brain
All these aspects of the environment must work together to build a better brain

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.992120/full

Cont…
In almost all countries or areas, more than half of children are engaged in early learning activities by adults in the household, but less than half have access to three or more books in home
Globally, less than 40% of infant- exclusively breastfed 
Violent discipline is widespread. Percentage of children aged 2 to 4 years who experience any violent discipline (psychological aggression and/or physical punishment)
Fewer than 50% of children  attending early childhood education programs in a majority of countries or areas    
      
        UNICEF/NYHQ SURVEY 2019

CHILD DEVELOPMENT
EXPERIENCE (nurture)  DIRECT EFFECT ON PHYSICAL GROWTH & PROPERTIES OF BRAIN (nature) 
Earlier experiences --- established synaptic pathways ---better learning
Experiences cause shifting of probabilities one way or  other

Cont…

Genetics 
In utero exposure to teratogens
Postnatal illnesses
Exposure to hazardous substances

Cont…
BIOLOGIC INFLUENCES ON DEVELOPMENT
Physical & neurological maturation sets  lower limits for emergence of most abilities
Hormonal influences are  basis for specific behavior (trigger, regulate, sustain)

Cont…
BIOLOGIC INFLUENCES ON DEVELOPMENT
TEMPERAMENT 
Child ’s characteristic behavioral response to internal & external stimuli
Biologically  determined
PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS

cont
PSYCHOLOGICAL INFLUENCES ON DEVELOPMENT
ATTACHMENT
Biologically  determined tendency of  young child to seek proximity to  parent during times of stress
Securely attached children use their parents to establish well being after  stressful experience

Cont…
PSYCHOLOGIC INFLUENCES ON DEVELOPMENT
CONTINGENCY
Contingent responses to non-verbal gestures create base for shared attention & reciprocity which are critical for later language & social development
SOCIAL FACTORS

Cont..
Human ecology evolves from “ assumption that humans are  part of  total life system & cannot be considered apart from all other living species in nature &  environments that surround them” (Andrews, Bubolz, & Paolucci, 1980, p. 32)
FAMILY SYSTEMS  & ECOLOGICAL MODEL Bronfenbrenner (1977)

TRANSACTIONAL MODEL, RISK AND RESILIENCE
Proposes  that child’s status at any point in time is  function of  interaction between biologic & social influences i.e.,  influences are bidirectional

Cont…
DEVELOPMENTAL DOMAINS
Gross motor development
Fine motor development
Communication & language development
Social / adaptive   
Cognitive development
Emotional development

Cont…
The development of child takes place in stages. Each stage has certain unique characteristics & in each stage, certain types of behavior or traits are more conspicuous than others. 
Entire period of development is divided into following stages
PRENATAL-PERIOD- It is mainly physiological and consists of growth of all body parts.

Cont..
INFANCY-  A period of newborn. Growth is temporarily at a standstill. 
 BABYHOOD- At this stage, the babies are completely helpless during the early part. Gradually they learn to control the muscles so that they can become independent.
CHILDHOOD- This period lasts from two to thirteen years of age. It is subdivided into two parts: 
EARLY CHILDHOOD- The child learns to gain control over the environment and starts learning to make social adjustments.
LATE CHILDHOOD- It is the period when sexual maturity occurs and adolescence begins. The major development is socialization.

Cont..
ADOLESCENCE- It is twelve years onwards till the individual assumes adulthood. It is again divided into two stages: 
EARLY ADOLESCENCE- Physical growth is rapid in both boys and girls. There is enhanced mental activity in general.
LATER ADOLECENCE- it is characterized by tapering off of physical growth but the psychological development continues in many complex ways preparing him to adjust to the demands of society as an adult. 
ADULTHOOD- By this time, physical changes are nearly complete but the psychological adjustments continue throughout the entire stage.

Cont…
OVERVIEW OF DEVELOPMENTAL PERIODS:
Prenatal period: from conception to birth
Infancy & toddlerhood: birth to 2 years
Early childhood: 2-6 years old
Middle childhood: 6-12 years old
Adolescence: 12-19 years old

Cont…
PERIODS OF DEVELOPMENT:

Young adulthood                          (20 to 40 years)
Middle adulthood                         (40 to 65 years )
Late adulthood                              (65 years and over)

topics.title: Growth and development
topics.core: Growth describes measurable physical change; development includes changing abilities across physical, cognitive, emotional and social life. Both should be studied over time.
points: Height and weight are growth measures.
Functional skills reveal development.
Human development includes change and stability from conception through later life.
topics.example: A child may gain height while also learning to take turns; these are related but different observations.

topics.title: A lifespan perspective
topics.core: Baltes’s framework treats development as lifelong, contextual and modifiable rather than a simple climb toward adulthood.
points: Gains and losses can coexist.
Biological and cultural influences change with age.
Resources are allocated differently across life.
Historical context shapes opportunities.
topics.example: An adolescent may gain independent reasoning while adjusting to new social demands.

topics.title: Domains and developmental periods
topics.core: Motor, communication, cognition, emotion and social/adaptive skills interact. Age periods organize study but do not create identical schedules for every child.
points: Prenatal life precedes birth.
Infancy and toddlerhood lead into preschool and school years.
Adolescence combines biological and social transitions.
Young, middle and later adulthood remain developmental periods.
topics.example: Putting on a shoe involves movement, understanding, motivation and adaptive independence.

topics.title: Brain development and experience
topics.core: Connections are formed, strengthened and reorganized through development and experience. Brain development does not stop at birth or at one preschool birthday.
points: Responsive interaction supports learning.
Nutrition and health support growth.
Safety and manageable stress support participation.
Synaptic pruning is selective reorganization, not a claim that connection numbers never change.
topics.example: Repeated back-and-forth play gives a child opportunities to practise attention and interaction.

topics.title: Biology and temperament
topics.core: Genes, prenatal exposures, illness, maturation and temperament contribute to development. None should be treated as the sole destiny of the child.
points: Teratogens can disrupt prenatal development.
Maturation supports readiness for new abilities.
Temperament describes characteristic responses.
Caregiving can adapt to individual differences.
topics.example: A cautious toddler may need more gradual introduction to an unfamiliar activity.

topics.title: Attachment and contingent interaction
topics.core: Attachment concerns an enduring emotional relationship; contingency means responding in a way connected to the child’s signals.
points: Comfort can support exploration.
Gestures can begin shared attention.
Reciprocity involves responding to one another.
Secure relationships are built through repeated interactions.
topics.example: An adult follows a baby’s gaze, names the toy and pauses for a response.

topics.title: Ecological and transactional models
topics.core: Development takes place in interacting family, school, community and cultural environments. Transactional accounts emphasize influence in both directions between children and caregivers.
points: Immediate settings matter.
Connections between settings matter.
Wider resources and policies affect families.
Child behavior can change adult responses and vice versa.
topics.example: A school routine changes family evenings, while family stress can influence classroom participation.

topics.title: Risk, resilience and the first 1,000 days
topics.core: The period from conception to the second birthday is a major opportunity for support, not the only opportunity to learn. Risks can accumulate, and protective relationships and resources matter.
points: Poverty can restrict opportunities without determining outcomes.
Malnutrition, illness and unsafe environments can compound risk.
Responsive care and stimulation are protective.
Historical prevalence estimates need their original year and denominator.
topics.example: A family support programme combines nutrition, caregiver wellbeing and opportunities for play.

milestones.text: Conception to birth; biological development occurs within a maternal and social context.
Birth through approximately two years; rapid change in movement, communication and interaction.
Preschool years; growing language, play, regulation and everyday independence.
School years; more organized learning, peer participation and complex movement.
Puberty, identity, abstract thought and increasing autonomy develop on overlapping trajectories.

questions.question: Which observation measures growth most directly?
questions.explanation: Growth refers to measurable physical change. For example, plotting height over time describes growth; taking turns describes social development.

questions.question: A child learns to dress independently. Which interpretation is best?
options: Domains develop without influencing each other
questions.explanation: Dressing combines coordination, understanding, sequencing and motivation. Developmental domains interact in everyday tasks.

questions.question: What is central to a lifespan view of development?
questions.explanation: Development includes gains, adjustments and losses across life. An adult learning a new skill is still developing.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates a contingent response?
options: An adult names the object the baby points toward
An adult repeats unrelated words continuously
An adult chooses all activities without observing the baby
questions.explanation: A contingent response connects to the child's signal. Naming a pointed-at toy supports shared attention.

questions.question: What does temperament describe?
questions.explanation: Temperament concerns typical responses such as approach, activity and reactivity. A cautious child may benefit from a gradual introduction.

questions.question: Which statement fits a transactional model?
options: Children and caregivers influence one another
A child's behavior never changes adult responses
questions.explanation: Influence moves in both directions. A baby's signals shape adult responses, which then influence the baby's experience.

questions.question: Which example illustrates an ecological influence?
options: Height increasing without any contextual influence
One test score determining the child's future
School and family routines affecting participation
questions.explanation: Ecological models consider connected settings. Consistent support at home and school may improve participation.

questions.question: What does resilience mean in development?
options: Positive adaptation in the presence of adversity
questions.explanation: Resilience is adaptation despite challenges. A supportive adult can be a protective factor during family disruption.

questions.question: How should brain development be understood?
options: Connections continue to be reorganized through experience
The brain is complete at birth
questions.explanation: Experience and maturation shape connections over time. Repeated language interaction provides practice for developing systems.

questions.question: What does the first 1,000 days emphasize?
options: A deadline after which learning is impossible
A period when caregiving has no influence
The period from conception through roughly the second birthday
Only the first 1,000 days after school entry
questions.explanation: This period highlights early nutrition, health and responsive care. It is an important opportunity, not a claim that later support cannot help.

clarifications.title: Reading the early-life claims
clarifications.text: Exclusive breastfeeding for about the first six months is a recommended feeding practice, not a developmental risk in itself. Brain connections and infant growth are dynamic. Historical population estimates in these slides should not be read as current statistics.

topics.title: Embryonic and fetal development
topics.core: Early development transforms a fertilized cell into an embryo and then a fetus. Organ formation and later growth have different vulnerabilities.
points: Germ layers give rise to body structures.
The embryonic period is sensitive to disruption.
Later fetal life includes growth and maturation.
Pregnancy dating and post-fertilization dating differ by about two weeks.
topics.example: An apparent timing disagreement may reflect different dating systems rather than a different biological event.

topics.title: Developing nervous system
topics.core: Neural structures emerge early, followed by extensive growth, connection formation and maturation. Having major structures at birth does not mean the brain is mature.
points: The neural tube contributes to the central nervous system.
Synapses continue changing after birth.
Myelination continues beyond early childhood in many pathways.
Hypoxia and harmful exposures can affect development.
topics.example: A newborn’s brain already supports interaction while later abilities still require maturation and experience.

topics.title: Fetal behavior and learning
topics.core: Movements, swallowing and responses to stimulation emerge before birth. Repeated stimulation can lead to habituation.
points: Movement is not equivalent to adult voluntary control.
Sensory experience contributes to learning.
Habituation means reduced response to repeated familiar stimulation.
Breathing-like movements do not mean fetal lungs breathe air.
topics.example: A reduced response across repeated presentations can indicate familiarization rather than simple lack of awareness.

topics.title: Transition to parenthood and prenatal risk
topics.core: Parents may experience excitement, uncertainty and increasing awareness of the fetus. These experiences vary across families rather than following compulsory emotional stages.
points: Fetal movement can affect parents’ sense of connection.
Mental health and practical support matter.
Infection, substances, illness and social adversity can raise risk.
A risk factor is not a diagnosis or inevitable outcome.
topics.example: A worried parent may benefit from supportive discussion rather than being told that attachment must feel a certain way.

topics.title: The newborn transition
topics.core: The neonatal period covers approximately the first 28 days. Feeding, circulation, temperature regulation, arousal and social interaction adapt to life outside the womb.
points: Record weight, length and head circumference.
Observe tone, spontaneous movement and responsiveness.
Newborn vision is limited but useful.
Hearing and interaction are present while processing continues to mature.
topics.example: A clinician considers the baby’s state and comfort when interpreting responsiveness.

topics.title: States and caregiver interaction
topics.core: Quiet sleep, active sleep, drowsiness, quiet alertness, active/fussy alertness and crying help organize observations of newborn behavior.
points: Arousal affects readiness to interact.
Caregivers can learn the infant’s signals.
Feeding and comfort needs affect state.
Quiet alert periods often support face-to-face engagement.
topics.example: An adult waits until a baby is calmly alert rather than treating every sleepy response as an inability.

topics.title: Reflexes: recognize the response
topics.core: Primitive reflexes support early function and provide information in a trained clinical examination. Some fade with maturation, while protective responses appear later.
points: Rooting turns the face toward feeding-related stimulation.
Moro includes an arm opening-and-return pattern.
Palmar and plantar grasp involve grasping responses.
Plantar grasp is not the Babinski response.
ATNR, Galant and oculocephalic responses have distinct patterns.
The parachute response appears later and persists.
topics.example: A student distinguishes curled toes in plantar grasp from an extending great toe in an infant plantar response; testing belongs to trained clinicians.

topics.title: Supporting the early relationship
topics.core: Prenatal circumstances, birth experiences and postnatal support influence interaction without determining attachment from one moment.
points: Support caregiver mental health.
Facilitate appropriate early contact and feeding support.
Rooming-in can create interaction opportunities.
A relationship can develop even when medical care delays initial contact.
topics.example: A family whose baby needs neonatal care can build closeness through supported interactions over time.

milestones.text: Cell division, implantation, germ-layer formation and early neural development.
Major organ formation; exact week labels require a stated dating convention.
Growth, sensory experience and ongoing organ maturation; 24 weeks does not mean mature lungs.
Physiological adaptation, state regulation, feeding and early reciprocal contact.
Eyes open with relatively low activity; useful opportunities for interaction.
Different behavioral and physiological patterns; do not confuse all movement with wakefulness.

questions.question: Why distinguish gestational age from age since fertilization?
options: They always differ by six months
questions.explanation: Gestational age is generally counted from the last menstrual period, about two weeks before fertilization. The dating convention changes the week label.

questions.question: Why can exposure timing matter during pregnancy?
options: Every exposure has the same effect
Timing eliminates the importance of dose
All organs form at the same instant
Different organs have sensitive periods of development
questions.explanation: Developing organs are vulnerable at different times. Timing, dose and other circumstances affect risk.

questions.question: Which statement about fetal lungs is most accurate?
options: They function exactly like adult lungs before birth
They are fully mature at 24 weeks in every fetus
They stop developing after the embryonic period
They continue maturing late in pregnancy
questions.explanation: Lungs mature progressively. Reaching a particular week does not mean a fetus has mature lungs or no risk from early birth.

questions.question: Which newborn state is usually useful for face-to-face interaction?
questions.explanation: A quietly alert baby is awake and relatively settled. This can provide a good opportunity for gentle interaction.

questions.question: What does rooting primarily support?
options: Protective arm extension during a fall
questions.explanation: Rooting turns the face toward stimulation near the mouth. It helps a newborn find a feeding source.

questions.question: Which response describes palmar grasp?
options: Turning the head toward cheek stimulation
Finger flexion around stimulation of the palm
questions.explanation: Palmar means the palm of the hand. A grasp response closes the fingers around an object contacting the palm.

questions.question: Why should plantar grasp and the Babinski response be distinguished?
options: They are identical names for rooting
Toe grasping differs from great-toe extension
questions.explanation: Plantar grasp involves toe flexion; the infant plantar response may include great-toe extension. Similar body location does not mean the same reflex.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the parachute response?
options: A protective response that appears later and persists
A reflex that must disappear in the first month
A feeding reflex present only before birth
questions.explanation: Protective extension develops later than many primitive newborn responses and persists. It is assessed by trained clinicians.

questions.question: What is the safest learning approach to neonatal reflexes?
options: Learn patterns and rely on trained clinical assessment
Assume all reflexes disappear at the same age
Practise dropping a baby to elicit Moro
questions.explanation: Reflex interpretation depends on the examination and age. Never create a fall or unsafe movement to test a response.

questions.question: A baby needs neonatal care and early contact is delayed. What follows?
options: A close relationship can still develop through supported interaction
Only the first hour determines all later relationships
questions.explanation: Relationships build through repeated care. Families can develop closeness even when medical circumstances delay initial contact.

clarifications.title: Prenatal dates and reflexes
clarifications.text: Gestational age and age since fertilization use different starting points. Lungs continue maturing late in pregnancy. Plantar grasp differs from the Babinski response. Reflex timing varies by source and context; these notes do not teach home reflex testing.

topics.title: Principles of motor development
topics.core: Gross motor skills involve posture and large movements; fine motor skills involve controlled hand and finger use. The two systems cooperate in daily tasks.
points: Cephalocaudal trends move from head control toward lower-body control.
General responses become more differentiated.
Rates vary across children.
Reflex integration supports voluntary movement.
topics.example: Reaching for a cup needs stable posture and coordinated hand control.

topics.title: Early gross motor sequence
topics.core: The lecture follows changing head control, prone support, rolling and sitting into later standing and mobility. Ages are approximate teaching anchors.
points: Head lag reduces as control improves.
Forearm support progresses toward straighter-arm support.
Sitting changes from supported to more independent.
Crawling patterns vary and are not an obligatory identical pathway.
topics.example: Observe the quality and symmetry of movement rather than assigning a diagnosis from one birthday.

topics.title: Walking, stairs and preschool movement
topics.core: Mobility becomes more independent and adaptable, then develops into running, stair negotiation, jumping, hopping and skipping.
points: Cruising differs from independent walking.
Support and step pattern matter on stairs.
Balance develops through practice and maturation.
Preschool coordination improves across several skills.
topics.example: Walking while holding furniture is not the same milestone as walking independently.

topics.title: Fine motor foundations
topics.core: Reaching, grasping, purposeful release and wrist rotation support later manipulation. Vision and postural control contribute to these activities.
points: Skills cooperate rather than develop in isolation.
Opportunities and safe objects matter.
Small objects can create choking hazards.
Manipulation supports exploration and self-care.
topics.example: Opening a container requires one hand to stabilize and the other to turn.

topics.title: From hand regard to manipulation
topics.core: Infants progress from early hand postures and looking to reaching, transferring, precision grasp and controlled release.
points: Visual tracking supports interaction.
A pincer grasp uses thumb and finger.
Early and refined grasps are different.
Scribbling and block play create practice opportunities.
topics.example: Picking up a safe large snack with precision differs from grasping a toy with the whole hand.

topics.title: Drawing, dressing and hand use
topics.core: Preschool tasks combine visual-motor control, finger coordination and learned routines. Figure copying becomes more complex but should not be treated as a universal age test by itself.
points: Circle, square and triangle copying increase in complexity.
Pencil control develops beyond one fixed grip label.
Dressing involves sequencing as well as dexterity.
Do not force a preferred writing hand.
topics.example: A child practises buttons with patient support and gradually needs less help.

topics.title: Variation, delay, deviancy and dissociation
topics.core: Delay concerns slower attainment; deviancy concerns an unusual pattern; dissociation concerns uneven development across domains. These descriptions guide further inquiry rather than name a diagnosis.
points: Consider opportunity, vision, tone and health.
Advanced movement does not prove higher intelligence.
Regression deserves prompt professional discussion.
Assess across settings and over time.
topics.example: A child strong in running but struggling with fine tasks needs a domain-specific profile, not a single global label.

topics.title: Assessment and the technoference assignment
topics.core: The slides introduce Gesell’s maturational observations and the Peabody motor scales. Standardized tools require the correct edition, administration and interpretation.
points: Separate gross and fine motor findings.
Observation and caregiver reports complement tools.
Screening is not diagnosis.
The assignment examines technology interrupting adult–child interaction, not simply all screen use.
topics.example: An adult silencing notifications during play can protect a back-and-forth interaction routine.

milestones.text: Progressive head control, prone support and reduction of head lag.
Rolling, sitting and increasing mobility; order and timing are not identical for all children.
Pulling up and cruising may precede independent steps; use milestone windows rather than an exact deadline.
Independent walking becomes more adaptable; running, kicking and stairs develop with support and practice.
Balance, jumping, hopping, tricycle use and more complex coordination are practised.
Reaching, grasping, transfer, precision grasp and deliberate release become more coordinated.
Scribbling, block construction, page turning and simple self-care provide practice.
More complex copying, cutting and fastenings develop; task conditions and experience matter.

questions.question: Which task is primarily fine motor?
questions.explanation: Fine motor tasks use precise hand and finger control. Buttoning also requires vision and sequencing.

questions.question: What does a cephalocaudal trend describe?
options: Control developing broadly from head toward lower body
Control developing only from feet upward
Fine motor skill always preceding head control
questions.explanation: Head control generally develops before later standing and walking. This describes a broad trend rather than an exact timetable.

questions.question: How does cruising differ from independent walking?
options: Cruising uses furniture or another support
Cruising means crawling on hands and knees
questions.explanation: A child moving along furniture is cruising. Walking independently requires taking steps without that support.

questions.question: Which observation best illustrates a pincer grasp?
options: Holding a large ball against the chest
Using thumb and finger to pick up an object
Grasping with the whole palm alone
questions.explanation: A pincer grasp uses the thumb and a finger for precision. Use safe objects because small objects can be choking hazards.

questions.question: A child skips crawling but develops other mobility skills. What is the best interpretation?
options: Consider the overall pattern and movement quality
Crawling absence alone proves a disorder
The child must have advanced intelligence
questions.explanation: Motor pathways vary. Assessment considers the full history, symmetry, function and progress rather than one isolated milestone.

questions.question: What does developmental dissociation describe?
questions.explanation: A child may have strong gross motor skills and weaker language skills. That uneven profile is dissociation and needs interpretation in context.

questions.question: What is developmental regression?
options: A temporary wish for help during one task
questions.explanation: Loss of established abilities warrants prompt professional discussion. For example, losing words previously used consistently differs from simply learning new words slowly.

questions.question: What is a suitable response to emerging hand preference?
options: Provide practice without forcing the opposite hand
Force every child to use the right hand
questions.explanation: Hand preference varies. Support comfortable, effective hand use rather than forcing a particular side.

questions.question: What is technoference in the lecture assignment?
options: Every use of technology for learning
questions.explanation: Technoference concerns interruptions, such as checking notifications during a child's attempt to engage. The interaction context matters.

questions.question: What distinguishes screening from diagnosis?
options: Screening identifies a need for closer assessment
Screening always establishes the final diagnosis
questions.explanation: A screening result flags possible concerns. A fuller assessment considers history, observations and appropriate tools before diagnostic conclusions.

clarifications.title: Milestones are windows
clarifications.text: Motor sequences and ages are teaching guides, not diagnostic cutoffs. Crawling pathways vary. Loss of established skills deserves professional discussion. Respectful modern terminology replaces outdated labels in the source wording.

topics.title: Infant growth patterns
topics.core: Weight, length and head circumference follow changing trajectories during infancy. The lecture’s doubling/tripling rules are rough teaching heuristics, not universal diagnostic thresholds.
points: Early weight loss needs context and follow-up.
Subsequent growth should be monitored serially.
Body proportions change.
Growth charts are more informative than one remembered number.
topics.example: A clinician plots repeated measurements rather than deciding wellbeing from a single weight.

topics.title: Toddler, preschool and school growth
topics.core: Growth usually slows after infancy while proportions, strength and coordination change. Appetite can fluctuate, but feeding quality remains important.
points: Legs lengthen relative to the trunk.
Gait and alignment change with maturation.
School-age stamina and complex movement increase.
Persistent or asymmetric concerns need contextual assessment.
topics.example: A toddler eating less than during rapid infant growth is considered alongside the overall trajectory.

topics.title: Adolescence and sexual maturation
topics.core: Puberty brings changes in secondary sexual characteristics and body composition. Sequence and timing vary; Tanner stages describe characteristics, not exact chronological age.
points: Breast budding and testicular enlargement are key early changes in their respective pathways.
Adrenal hair changes are not identical to gonadal puberty.
Growth acceleration and voice changes can occur.
Five-stage ratings assess different features separately.
topics.example: A student separates pubic-hair staging from breast or genital staging rather than assigning one age from appearance.

topics.title: Dental development
topics.core: Teeth form, erupt and are later shed according to variable patterns. Primary and permanent dentitions have different schedules.
points: Primary teeth number 20.
Permanent first molars commonly emerge around six to seven years.
Premolars do not simply replace that first-molar milestone.
Delayed eruption or enamel changes have several possible explanations.
topics.example: A tooth-eruption chart supports learning better than assuming every child follows one exact month.

topics.title: Skeletal maturation
topics.core: Bone maturation can provide information about progress toward physical maturity. Bone age and chronological age are different measures.
points: Assessment uses appropriate reference standards.
Interpretation considers growth and puberty.
An estimate does not guarantee exact adult height.
Imaging is a clinical decision, not a home developmental test.
topics.example: Two children of the same age can differ in skeletal maturation.

topics.title: Measurement and growth charts
topics.core: Measure carefully, record accurately and interpret a series using an appropriate chart. Weight, recumbent length or standing height, and head circumference answer different questions.
points: Technique and equipment affect readings.
Percentiles describe a reference distribution.
A percentile alone is not a diagnosis.
Trajectory, family history and clinical context matter.
topics.example: An unexpected plotted change should first prompt checking measurement and context.

topics.title: Patterns that need assessment
topics.core: Weight, linear growth, head growth and puberty can deviate for nutritional, familial, endocrine or other medical reasons. The slide lists are examples rather than one-to-one diagnoses.
points: Distinguish undernutrition and excess weight patterns.
Short stature can be familial or illness-related.
Large head size does not alone prove hydrocephalus.
Early or late puberty needs an individual assessment.
topics.example: A pattern across height, weight and symptoms is more informative than guessing a syndrome from stature.

topics.title: Growth as a proxy: use and limits
topics.core: Physical growth can flag health and social risk but is not a complete measure of cognition, language or social development. Historical risk estimates should retain their original date and definition.
points: Association is not equivalence.
Development requires direct domain-specific observation.
Monitoring can be integrated with primary care.
The assignment asks for a referenced 1,500–2,000-word analysis of the proxy claim.
topics.example: A child’s expected height does not establish that language comprehension is developing as expected.

milestones.text: Rapid growth with changing velocity; interpret serial measures, not a single doubling rule.
Slower growth and changing body proportions can accompany variable appetite.
Steady progression, changing dentition and increasing physical strength.
Secondary sexual characteristics and growth acceleration; sequence and timing vary.
Prepubertal secondary sexual characteristics.
Early changes: breast budding or testicular/scrotal enlargement; pubic hair is assessed separately.
Further enlargement and development; different features may not share the same stage.
Advanced maturation; breast areola/papilla may form a secondary mound in the breast-rating system.
Mature secondary sexual characteristics; stage is not a precise age calculator.

questions.question: Why are serial growth measurements useful?
options: They show the child's trajectory over time
questions.explanation: A pattern across visits is more informative than one point. An unexpected change should be checked and interpreted with the clinical context.

questions.question: How should an infant weight-doubling rule be used?
options: As proof that feeding is always adequate
As a substitute for growth charts
questions.explanation: Doubling rules summarize typical patterns but do not fit every infant. Appropriate growth standards and the clinical picture are more useful.

questions.question: A newborn has substantial weight loss. What is the best response?
options: Assess feeding, hydration and clinical circumstances
Diagnose a lifelong growth disorder from one weight
questions.explanation: Early weight loss needs context. A concerning amount or associated symptoms requires assessment rather than automatic reassurance.

questions.question: What do Tanner stages describe?
questions.explanation: Tanner staging describes features such as breast or genital development and pubic hair. It is not an intelligence or school achievement scale.

questions.question: Which teeth commonly appear around early school age?
options: All permanent premolars before age three
A new set of primary incisors
questions.explanation: First permanent molars commonly erupt around six to seven years. Dental timing varies and should not be confused with premolar eruption.

questions.question: What is bone age used to estimate?
questions.explanation: Bone age assesses skeletal maturity, often using an appropriate radiograph. It is interpreted alongside growth and other clinical information.

questions.question: Why can measurement technique matter?
options: Poor positioning can distort height or length
questions.explanation: Accurate positioning and calibrated equipment support valid measurements. An apparent growth change can sometimes reflect measurement error.

questions.question: Can physical growth alone represent all development?
options: No, functional and contextual information is also needed
Yes, puberty stage determines social skills
questions.explanation: Growth is one important dimension. Communication, learning, relationships and daily functioning require their own observations.

questions.question: Which statement about brain maturation is appropriate?
options: All myelination ends at age five
Brain development ends when teeth erupt
It continues beyond the early school years
questions.explanation: Brain systems mature over an extended period. One early-childhood age cannot mark completion of every process.

questions.question: What is a sound approach to a growth concern?
options: Diagnose solely from comparison with a sibling
Verify measurements and assess the pattern and context
Use a single unreferenced age rule
questions.explanation: Check technique, plot appropriate measurements and consider health, feeding and family history. One comparison cannot supply the full explanation.

clarifications.title: Growth rules need context
clarifications.text: Weight-doubling rules and dental ages are approximations. Substantial newborn weight loss needs clinical assessment. Myelination does not finish universally at age five to seven. First permanent molars generally precede premolars. Physical growth alone cannot represent every developmental domain.

Points to objects

topics.title: Communication has several channels
topics.core: Communication exchanges information through language and other signals. Speech is one way of expressing language, not its entire definition.
points: Gestures, posture and eye contact can communicate.
Signed and written languages are linguistic systems.
Tone and rhythm contribute paralinguistic information.
Avoid equating all communication with spoken words.
topics.example: A child points, looks toward a caregiver and vocalizes to request a toy.

topics.title: Speech, comprehension and expression
topics.core: Speech involves producing spoken sounds; language concerns structured meaning. Receptive language concerns understanding, while expressive language concerns producing messages.
points: Motor coordination supports spoken output.
Comprehension can exceed spoken vocabulary.
Production can be spoken, signed or written.
The slide’s production paragraph mistakenly repeats understanding of written language.
topics.example: A child can understand give me the cup before saying a comparable sentence.

topics.title: Hearing and listening
topics.core: Hearing provides auditory access; listening involves attention, selection, memory and interpretation. Auditory processing continues to develop after birth.
points: Localization concerns identifying sound direction.
Acoustic and contextual evidence contribute.
Early recognition does not equal adult-level processing.
A hearing concern warrants appropriate assessment rather than assumptions.
topics.example: A child may detect a sound yet struggle to follow a complex spoken instruction.

topics.title: Prelinguistic foundations
topics.core: Turn-taking, joint attention, gestures, cooing and babbling create foundations for later language. They are meaningful developmental achievements before first words.
points: Joint attention involves shared focus.
Babbling includes speech-like sound play.
Gestures can request and share interest.
Adult responses support reciprocal routines.
topics.example: An adult follows the infant’s pointing and comments on the same object.

topics.title: First words and toddler communication
topics.core: Meaningful words emerge alongside gestures and growing comprehension. Vocabulary and combinations develop with considerable individual and language variation.
points: Receptive and expressive vocabulary are not identical.
First words need communicative meaning, not perfect adult pronunciation.
Early combinations build new messages.
The course’s numerical vocabulary estimates are not standalone diagnostic cutoffs.
topics.example: More milk communicates a combination of meanings beyond naming milk alone.

topics.title: Preschool language
topics.core: Children increasingly ask questions, use grammatical patterns, tell events and follow more complex messages. Intelligibility depends on listener, language, context and measurement.
points: Pronouns, tense and plurals develop progressively.
Stories become richer.
Do not equate sentence word count with age.
MLU is an average calculated from a language sample, with the counting unit specified.
topics.example: Compare several utterances when examining grammatical complexity rather than counting one sentence.

topics.title: School language and literacy
topics.core: Oral language supports reading, spelling, writing and academic participation. Later development includes more organized narratives, abstract vocabulary and figurative meanings.
points: Written language is produced as well as understood.
Oral-language difficulty can affect literacy.
Support must reflect language and learning context.
School-age abilities continue developing beyond basic conversation.
topics.example: A learner can speak conversationally yet need help explaining a science concept in writing.

topics.title: A language-supportive environment
topics.core: Responsive conversation, shared reading and opportunities to express ideas help learning. Interaction matters more than merely exposing a child to background speech.
points: Follow the child’s interests.
Pause for a response.
Expand rather than shame an attempt.
Use familiar languages and meaningful routines.
topics.example: During picture-book reading, ask an accessible question and build on the child’s answer.

milestones.text: Crying, early vocalization, attention to voices and reciprocal engagement.
Vocal play and early babbling expand alongside responsiveness and interaction.
Gesture, imitation, familiar-word understanding and speech-like babbling become more developed.
Meaningful words, growing comprehension and emerging combinations expand communication.
Questions, grammar, narrative and understanding of more complex instructions develop.
Conversation links increasingly with literacy, organized explanation and figurative or abstract language.
Detection, localization, attention, interpretation and language understanding are related but different skills.

questions.question: Which example is receptive language?
questions.explanation: Receptive language concerns understanding. Following “put the cup on the table” shows comprehension rather than spoken expression.

questions.question: Which example is expressive language?
options: Using words or signs to communicate an idea
questions.explanation: Expression conveys meaning through spoken, signed or written forms. A child signing “more” communicates expressively.

questions.question: How does speech differ from language?
options: Speech and language always mean identical things
Speech is one means of producing a language message
questions.explanation: Speech concerns sound production and related processes; language is a system for meaning. A child can use language through signs without speech.

questions.question: What does mean length of utterance summarize?
options: Average utterance length in specified linguistic units
The number of conversations per day
questions.explanation: MLU averages units such as morphemes or words across utterances. It is not simply another name for age.

questions.question: Which caregiver action supports early communication?
options: Follow the child's interest and take conversational turns
Avoid gestures until speech is perfect
questions.explanation: Responsive turns connect words with attention and meaning. Naming a toy, pausing and responding creates a useful learning exchange.

questions.question: Why does hearing assessment matter when language is delayed?
options: Access to sound can affect communication learning
All language delays prove hearing loss
questions.explanation: Hearing differences are one possible influence on communication. Assessment helps distinguish contributing factors without assuming a single cause.

questions.question: What is joint attention?
options: Measuring the loudness of a voice
Sharing attention to an object or event with another person
Repeating an isolated sound during sleep
questions.explanation: A child looks between an adult and an interesting toy or follows a point. Shared attention supports opportunities to connect meaning and communication.

questions.question: Which is a prelinguistic communication behavior?
options: Using a gesture to request something
questions.explanation: Gestures, gaze and early vocalizations communicate before fluent words. Reaching toward a caregiver can express a request.

questions.question: How should vocabulary counts at a specific age be interpreted?
options: As identical requirements for every language learner
As unrelated to opportunities for communication
As context-dependent indicators alongside other information
questions.explanation: Language exposure, measurement and individual variation matter. A useful assessment considers understanding, gestures, progress and everyday function as well as words.

questions.question: How are language and literacy connected?
options: Literacy begins without any language foundation
Spoken or signed language skills support later reading and writing
Speech clarity alone guarantees reading mastery
questions.explanation: Vocabulary, narrative and sound or language awareness support literacy. Reading also requires specific instruction and practice.

clarifications.title: Communication terminology
clarifications.text: Written expression means writing; understanding written language is comprehension. MLU is an average length in specified linguistic units, not chronological age. Vocabulary counts and intelligibility figures require language and assessment context. Auditory development continues after birth.

EMOTIONAL             DEVELOPMENT
BY
Dr. ASMA SHABBIR
ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR
PEDIATRICS, IIMC-T

EMOTIONAL DEVELOPMENT
Definition of emotion as feeling or affect that occurs when person is engaged in an interaction that is important to her or him especially to their wellbeing
Characterized by behavior that reflects (expresses) pleasantness or unpleasantness of state individuals are in , or transactions they are experiencing
Specific  &  vary, adopted by Joseph Campos(2005)

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8645455_On_the_Nature_of_Emotion_Regulation

EMOTIONAL DEVELOPMENT
Involves   recognition & expression of feelings & emotions.

EMOTIONAL DEVELOPMENT
Emotional development,  refers to child’s  ability to
Recognize  & understand their own feelings
Accurately  interpret  feelings of others
Manage  the way they feel
Shape  the way they behave

Cont..
Develop  Empathy 
Build & maintain good relationships with family, friends & others
From birth, children quickly develop their abilities to experience & express different emotions, as well as their capacity to cope with & manage variety of feelings

Cont..
Pleasure , distress, anger, surprise, interest, disgust, sadness & fear  classified as “basic emotions” (Dragh-Lorenz, 2001).

Basic emotions are experienced by human beings & each consists of three elements

Subjective  feeling
Physiological  change
Overt  behavior

Cont..
Emotions determined in infants by Facial expressions
Provide  important clues about which emotion  child is experiencing-facial expressions accurately reflect an infant’s emotional state
Research has shown that infants worldwide express basic emotions in  same way-Izard et al.,(1995-2024)
Humans have universal emotional expression & biologically programmed to express emotions in a specific way

Cont..
Reflexive Smile
     Birth to 3-4 weeks 
     Spontaneous, not in response to any stimulus


Social smile
     6-8 weeks: Smile in response to external 
     elicitors bouncing, especially faces

Cont..
Early emotional development
Development of emotions more psychologically (cognitively) based with age 
Like distress versus anger: Distress has no cognitive component; newborns  distressed if feel pain, but don't direct anger at  specific person inflicting pain until later in  first year

Cont..
Fear does not develop until 7 months of age; requires cognitive ability to differentiate between familiar versus unfamiliar people
Emotions  more contextually sensitive with age, infants respond emotionally to meaning of  situation

Cont..
Two types of emotions:
Primary emotions (Startle, Distress, Happiness, fear)
Secondary emotions (Shame, Pride, Guilt) require more cognitive sophistication
Rapid changes & more discrete emotions  develop, by nine months infants are thought to experience all basic emotions

Cont..
Research suggests complex emotions depend on  child having self-awareness & consciousness of adult reactions (Lewis, 2000).
Self-awareness-foundation  for emotional development is realization that we are distinct individuals- separate from other people
Emerging  sense of “me” & “mine” fosters self-conscious emotions

Cont..
Attachment an enduring emotional connection
A close emotional bond that is “person-specific” & enduring across time & space (Ainsworth,1970)
Infants show their attachment through proximity-seeking behaviors, meaning infants (and adults) like to be near those  attached
Certain Actions as well as contact-maintaining behaviors all  evidence of attachment.

Cont..
Harlow showed development of attachment closely associated with critical periods in early life, after which difficult or impossible to compensate for loss of initial emotional security
According to theories of John Bowlby (1969, 1991),  children who form an attachment to an adult more likely to survive in emotionally enhanced manner
Attachment not only deepens parent-child relationship, may have contributed to human survival

Cont..
According to Bowlby, attachment progresses in four phases:

Pre-attachment
Attachment-in-the-Making
True (or Clear-cut) Attachment
Reciprocal Relationships

Cont..
Pre-attachment(0-6 weeks)
Infant  produces innate signals (crying, clinging, smiling, or sucking) that bring others to his/her side & infant  comforted by these interactions
Infant’s behaviors & response evoke from adults creates an interactive system that is  first step in  formation of attachment

Cont..
Attachment-in-Making (6-8 months)
Infants begin to respond preferentially to familiar people
Infants forming expectations about how their caregivers will respond to their needs & as a result, develop (or not) a sense of trust in them

Cont..

topics.title: Emotions and emotional development
topics.core: Emotional development includes recognizing, expressing and managing feelings, understanding others and building relationships. Feelings, physiological responses and behavior are connected but not identical.
points: Pleasure, distress, interest and fear are examples of early emotion categories.
Self-conscious emotions involve additional self-awareness.
Expression is one clue, not an infallible mind-reading tool.
Empathy develops through interaction and learning.
topics.example: An adult notices a child’s posture and situation rather than labeling one facial movement with certainty.

topics.title: Early emotional expression
topics.core: Reflexive smiling and socially responsive smiling differ. Emotional patterns become more differentiated and context-sensitive across development.
points: Early smiles can occur without a social partner.
Social smiling emerges in early interaction.
Do not impose one exact month when all fear begins.
Individual differences and caregiver responses matter.
topics.example: A caregiver responds to a baby’s emerging social smile with a brief face-to-face exchange.

topics.title: Attachment phases
topics.core: Bowlby’s teaching model moves from early signaling to selective preference, clear attachment and more reciprocal relationships. The phases are approximate, not compulsory deadlines.
points: Early signals attract care.
Familiar people gain importance.
A secure base supports exploration.
Language and perspective-taking later support negotiation about separation.
topics.example: A toddler checks back with a familiar caregiver while exploring a new room.

topics.title: Relationships and responsive care
topics.core: Attachment is enduring and person-specific; it is not proof of one perfect birth moment or a child’s temperament score. Relationships remain capable of change.
points: Contact-seeking can communicate distress.
Consistency and sensitivity matter.
Multiple trusted caregivers can contribute.
Historical deprivation studies do not justify claims that later support is useless.
topics.example: A child in a new caregiving arrangement can build trust through repeated responsive care.

topics.title: Temperament and goodness of fit
topics.core: Temperament describes characteristic patterns of reactivity and regulation. It interacts with experience rather than fixing a permanent personality fate.
points: Observe intensity and adaptability.
Adjust routines to the individual.
Do not label a cautious child as disobedient.
Caregiver interpretation affects the interaction.
topics.example: A slower-to-warm child receives time to observe before joining a group.

topics.title: Wariness, separation and social referencing
topics.core: Infants may show stranger wariness or separation distress as recognition and mobility develop. Social referencing uses another person’s emotional signals to interpret uncertainty.
points: Timing and intensity vary.
Distress is not automatically an attachment disorder.
A calm familiar adult can provide cues.
Social referencing is related to, but not identical with, theory of mind.
topics.example: An infant checks a parent’s face before approaching an unfamiliar toy.

topics.title: Autonomy and tantrums
topics.core: Growing independence can exceed a toddler’s language and inhibitory control. Adults can co-regulate while maintaining clear, developmentally appropriate limits.
points: Words can gradually support self-regulation.
Fatigue and frustration affect behavior.
Avoid treating one duration or frequency as a diagnosis.
Persistent, severe or harmful patterns deserve professional discussion.
topics.example: A caregiver names frustration and offers a safe choice while keeping a limit.

topics.title: Preschool regulation and empathy
topics.core: Children practise labeling emotions, tolerating limits and handling peer conflict. External guidance gradually supports more internal regulation.
points: Predictable routines help.
Overly harsh or inconsistent responses can hinder learning.
Imaginary play is not automatically pathology.
Empathic responses and repair can be modelled.
topics.example: A teacher helps a child say I am upset instead of hitting.

topics.title: Moral reasoning and adolescence
topics.core: The lecture introduces Kohlberg’s preconventional, conventional and postconventional levels. These are a theory of reasoning, not fixed diagnostic ages or proof of moral worth.
points: Early reasoning may focus on consequences.
Social approval and order become relevant.
Principles and rights can organize later arguments.
Adolescents negotiate belonging, values and independence.
topics.example: Two students may support the same action for different reasons, which matters in analysing moral reasoning.

milestones.text: Distress, interest, soothing and emerging social smiling support exchanges.
Selective preferences, stranger wariness and separation responses may become more apparent.
Autonomy can outpace language and inhibition; adults support co-regulation.
Emotion labeling, perspective-taking, empathy and limit negotiation develop through practice.
Self-evaluation, achievement and belonging influence feelings and motivation.
Identity, peers, future concerns and increasingly complex regulation interact.
Kohlberg: reasoning organized around consequences and self-interest; not a fixed age diagnosis.
Kohlberg: reasoning organized around relationships, approval and social order.
Kohlberg: reasoning may appeal to rights, social contracts and principles; not an inevitable endpoint.

questions.question: What is co-regulation?
options: An adult refusing all emotional support
An adult helping a child manage arousal and feelings
A baby independently suppressing every emotion
questions.explanation: Young children rely on another person's calm and support. Naming a feeling and helping a child settle provides a foundation for later self-regulation.

questions.question: What does attachment primarily concern?
questions.explanation: Attachment involves the child's relationship with a caregiver, including seeking comfort and using that relationship to support exploration.

questions.question: Which response is sensitive to temperament?
options: Treat shyness as proof of low intelligence
Introduce a cautious child gradually to a new setting
Require all children to react identically
questions.explanation: Temperament describes characteristic responses. Gradual introductions can help a cautious child participate without assigning a negative label.

questions.question: A toddler looks at a caregiver before approaching an unfamiliar toy. What is this?
questions.explanation: Social referencing uses another person's emotional cues to guide behavior. A calm caregiver response may help the toddler approach.

questions.question: What is a constructive response to a tantrum?
options: Provide safety, calm support and consistent limits
Assume one tantrum establishes a diagnosis
Demand a complex explanation during peak distress
questions.explanation: A distressed child often needs help settling before reasoning. Afterward, simple language and consistent routines can support learning.

questions.question: How should stranger wariness be interpreted?
options: In relation to age, temperament and context
As proof of an insecure relationship
questions.explanation: Wariness varies. A child may need time with an unfamiliar person, especially when tired or in a new setting.

questions.question: Which behavior supports emerging autonomy?
questions.explanation: Limited choices let a child practise agency within safe boundaries. Choosing between two shirts supports independence without removing structure.

questions.question: What is a limitation of Kohlberg's stages?
options: They are a theory of moral reasoning rather than a fixed timetable for every person
They prove all adolescents reason identically
questions.explanation: The theory organizes types of justification for moral choices. Culture, context and the limits of the model matter when applying it.

questions.question: Which example illustrates emotion labeling?
options: Saying “You feel disappointed because playtime ended”
Telling a child all feelings are wrong
questions.explanation: Naming feelings connects experience with language. A caregiver can validate disappointment while keeping the bedtime limit.

questions.question: Can one facial expression establish an infant's exact emotion?
options: No, behavior and context must be considered
Yes, smiling rules out every difficulty
Yes, expressions always have one meaning
questions.explanation: Expressions are clues rather than perfect readouts. Crying may accompany hunger, fatigue, discomfort or distress.

clarifications.title: Emotional development is contextual
clarifications.text: A facial expression cannot reveal an exact emotion with certainty. Attachment builds over repeated interactions and later support can help. Fear and tantrum patterns vary. Kohlberg is a theoretical framework, not a compulsory age schedule. Social referencing is distinct from a full theory of mind.

topics.title: Cognition, working memory and expertise
topics.core: Cognition includes perceiving, remembering, reasoning and understanding. Working memory and accumulated knowledge help explain changes in performance.
points: Prior experience supports new learning.
Familiarity can reduce task demands.
Development varies across contexts.
Performance is not explained by age alone.
topics.example: A child solves a familiar puzzle more easily than an equally complex unfamiliar one.

topics.title: Piaget’s four stages
topics.core: The classical sequence is sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational. It is a theoretical framework rather than a rigid universal timetable.
points: Sensorimotor learning links action and perception.
Preoperational thought uses symbols but can be perceptually centered.
Concrete operations support conservation and reversibility.
Formal operations involve abstract or hypothetical reasoning.
topics.example: A conservation task examines whether changed appearance is confused with changed amount.

topics.title: Early learning and habituation
topics.core: Infants attend to visual, tactile, auditory and other information. Repetition and exploration reveal learning before spoken explanations are possible.
points: Habituation is reduced response to a repeated stimulus.
Novelty can renew attention.
Looking does not directly reveal every concept.
Repeated self-produced actions create experience.
topics.example: An infant repeatedly moves a hand while watching its changing position.

topics.title: Object exploration and permanence
topics.core: Object permanence concerns understanding that an object continues to exist when out of sight. Searching and looking-time tasks provide different evidence.
points: Infants inspect, transfer and manipulate objects.
Occlusion tasks need careful interpretation.
Failure to search can reflect motor or memory demands.
No single task fixes the exact age of all object knowledge.
topics.example: A hidden toy can be studied through search behavior or attention to an unexpected event.

topics.title: Toddler problem solving
topics.core: Mobility broadens exploration, and object use, anticipation, sorting and pretend routines become more complex.
points: In/out and part/whole relations develop.
Meaningful object use supports learning.
Imitation and make-believe differ from random manipulation.
Opportunities and familiarity affect performance.
topics.example: A child uses a toy cup in a pretend tea routine and sorts blocks by one property.

topics.title: Preschool thought and play
topics.core: Symbolic play expands into scenarios and roles. Egocentrism means difficulty taking another viewpoint, not simply selfishness.
points: Animism attributes lifelike qualities to objects.
Magical thinking can confuse wishes with causes.
Play supports practice and expression.
Understanding may exceed what a difficult task reveals.
topics.example: A child pretends a box is a bus and negotiates passenger roles.

topics.title: School readiness and self-efficacy
topics.core: School tasks increasingly demand attention, language processing and organized practice. Beliefs about competence and opportunities to succeed influence participation.
points: Reading, writing and number skills become central.
Task demands should be scaffolded.
External and internal motivations can coexist.
Repeated failure can reduce willingness to try without establishing fixed inability.
topics.example: A teacher breaks a challenging task into achievable steps and gives specific feedback.

topics.title: Adolescent reasoning
topics.core: Abstract and hypothetical reasoning, metacognition and planning can develop unevenly. Emotion and familiarity influence whether a skill is used in a situation.
points: Reasoning about thinking is metacognition.
Consequences and alternatives can be compared.
No unsupported percentage is a universal attainment rate.
Individual variation is more useful than assuming one sex always develops earlier.
topics.example: A student reasons logically about a science task but needs support in a stressful peer decision.

milestones.text: Approximately birth–2 years in the classical model: action, perception and developing object permanence.
Approximately 2–7 years: symbols and pretend play with limits in some logical tasks.
Approximately 7–11 years: conservation and reversible operations with concrete information.
Approximately 11 years onward in the classical account: hypothetical and abstract reasoning, with substantial task-dependent variation.
Habituation, sensory exploration, imitation and object manipulation offer evidence of cognition.
Make-believe expands into roles and scenarios; play supports problem-solving and social learning.
Increasing attention and curriculum demands interact with language, motivation and opportunities.
Metacognition, alternatives and future planning develop unevenly across situations.

questions.question: What is working memory?
options: A reflex present only at birth
questions.explanation: Working memory supports tasks such as remembering two instructions while carrying them out. It differs from permanent long-term storage.

questions.question: What is object permanence?
options: Assuming hidden objects have vanished permanently
Knowing the name of every object
Understanding that an object continues to exist when hidden
questions.explanation: Searching for a hidden toy illustrates the developing idea that it still exists. Performance depends on task demands as well as understanding.

questions.question: In Piaget's account, what is assimilation?
options: Changing a scheme to fit new information
Interpreting an experience using an existing scheme
questions.explanation: Calling a new four-legged animal “dog” can reflect use of an existing scheme. Accommodation would involve revising that scheme.

questions.question: What is accommodation in Piaget's theory?
options: Using an unchanged scheme for everything
Modifying a scheme when experience does not fit
questions.explanation: Learning that a cat differs from a dog may require adjusting categories. The child changes the existing mental organization.

questions.question: Which example illustrates symbolic play?
options: Tracking a moving light without pretending
Using a block as a pretend telephone
Dropping a toy only to hear a sound
questions.explanation: In symbolic play, one thing represents another. A block can stand for a phone even though it is not one.

questions.question: A child says a taller glass must contain more after water is poured into it. Which concept is relevant?
questions.explanation: Conservation concerns quantities remaining the same despite a changed appearance. A child may focus on height and overlook the narrower width.

questions.question: What distinguishes hypothetical reasoning?
options: Relying only on directly visible objects
Considering what would follow if a proposed condition were true
Repeating an answer without considering possibilities
questions.explanation: Hypothetical reasoning explores possibilities, such as predicting outcomes of different experimental conditions. It varies by knowledge and task.

questions.question: What is self-efficacy?
options: A measure of infant reflex strength
Belief in one's capacity to perform a task
A guarantee of success in every task
The number of years at school
questions.explanation: A student who believes practice can help them solve a problem has task-related confidence. Appropriate feedback and achievable steps can support it.

questions.question: Why should Piagetian ages be treated as approximate?
options: Task demands and experience affect performance
All abilities appear on a fixed birthday
Age removes the need to observe reasoning
Every child fits every stage exactly
questions.explanation: The stage framework is a useful teaching model with limitations. Children may demonstrate different abilities across tasks and contexts.

questions.question: How can expertise affect memory?
options: Knowledge can help organize and retrieve information
Experts have unlimited memory for everything
questions.explanation: A child familiar with a game may remember meaningful game patterns well. Expertise helps organize information within that domain.

clarifications.title: Use cognitive theories thoughtfully
clarifications.text: Piagetian ages organize a theory rather than set fixed diagnostic boundaries. Object-permanence tasks have different demands. Counting skills can emerge before age seven. A fixed attention span or unsupported percentage of people reaching formal operations should not be treated as a universal fact.

Social / Adaptive Development 
Social development is related to  Social, Emotional & Personal development of an individual
Infant begins taking in information through  senses, she/he must begin  process of interpreting & giving meaning to that information - called Perceptual development

Cont…
Earliest  pattern or object for focus of interest, & instrumental in learning in an infant’s life is  human face
Before an infant can  comprehend language or  environment,  begins to understand  meaning of certain expressions on  primary caregiver's face
Visual social cues signal  infant information about  perceiving world, whether joy, fear, apprehension, or another human emotion that is being expressed by  caregiver

Cont…
Refers  to  range of behaviors  child acquires during  developmental process to function independently
Sub-domains comprise of Self Care, Community Self-sufficiency, Personal-social Responsibility  & Social Adjustment
Advance  delineation results in  form of dressing/undressing, eating/feeding, toileting  & grooming, appropriate behavior in different settings, adjusting to new situations, & attending appropriately

Cont…
Adaptive behaviors are learned & involve ability to adapt to & manage one's surroundings to effectively function & meet social or community expectations.
Good adaptive behavior promotes independence.
Socially unacceptable behaviors that interfere with  acquisition of desired skills & performance  of everyday activities are classified as maladaptive behaviors.
Maladaptive behavior interferes with child's achievement of independence as child requires more supervision & assistance in order to learn appropriate behavior.

Cont…
Social  aspect of  development relates specifically to  interaction of people, dependent on  different social situations that the individual is subjected to
In contrast,  emotional side of  development relates to understanding & ability to control one’s emotions, which again is dependent on  situation
Both  emotional   &  social  development relate specifically to internal & external progression of individual

Cont…
Both  social & emotional concept of development is measured during a child’s growth which is split up into different stages
At each stage  child should be demonstrating a different aspect of social development  
Older  the child, more progressed this social development should appear

Cont…
In  terms of social development , growth is evaluated based on the different behavioral  characteristics
These behaviors will reflect child’s growth & level of understanding while progressing into adulthood  
Good social development imperative, as progression determine their social skills - allowing them to display proper reactions to specific social/emotional situations

Cont....

New-born help adults succeed as caregivers by being Readable , Predictable & Responsive
Social referencing- searching for cues to help interpret situation from care-givers or communicating  partners
Infants  generally use parent’s expressions as signals to guide their interpretations & reactions to various  events & situations
