topics.title: Social and adaptive skills
topics.core: Social development concerns participation with others; adaptive behavior concerns managing everyday demands and independence in context.
points: Self-care and social responsibility are related but distinct.
Expectations reflect age, culture and opportunity.
A difficulty is not a moral defect.
Support can improve access and participation.
topics.example: A child learns both how to put on a coat and when to ask for help.

topics.title: Faces and social referencing
topics.core: Infants attend to faces and use partners’ expressions as information. A caregiver’s signal is interpreted within a situation rather than read as a perfect emotion label.
points: Shared attention supports learning.
Responsive partners create reciprocal routines.
Infants are active participants.
Perception and social interpretation develop together.
topics.example: A child looks toward a familiar adult before approaching an unfamiliar object.

topics.title: Early social interaction
topics.core: The lecture traces face regard, social smiling, vocal exchange, imitation, gesture games and response to familiar people. Timing is approximate.
points: Mirror interest is not proof of full self-recognition.
Mouthing can be exploration.
Pointing can request or share interest.
Frustration can accompany restrictions.
topics.example: A baby alternates vocalizing with a caregiver during a simple game.

topics.title: Toddler self-care
topics.core: Feeding, cup use, dressing participation and indicating needs develop through practice and support. Toileting readiness is individual, and nighttime dryness is not an automatic two-year expectation.
points: Offer safe opportunities.
Separate independence from perfect performance.
Model routines step by step.
Do not punish accidents as intentional misconduct.
topics.example: A toddler helps with dressing before managing the whole sequence alone.

topics.title: Preschool peers and play
topics.core: Sharing, turn-taking, rules and household participation become more practiced. These abilities remain context-sensitive and need adult scaffolding.
points: Cooperative play develops gradually.
Storytelling can mix imagination and experience.
Rules may be interpreted from a child’s viewpoint.
Avoid expecting perfect sharing at one birthday.
topics.example: An adult coaches two children to alternate turns rather than labeling one unsuccessful attempt as a fixed trait.

topics.title: Everyday regulation
topics.core: Sleep, eating and toileting involve physiological needs, routines, emotional security and learned skills.
points: Seek patterns rather than blame.
Consider comfort, access and communication.
Support families with realistic expectations.
Persistent concerns require appropriate discussion.
topics.example: A predictable bedtime routine can support settling without implying that all sleep difficulties are behavioral.

topics.title: Middle-childhood relationships and values
topics.core: Teachers, peers, community experiences and media broaden the child’s social world. Belonging, prosocial behavior and moral reasoning become important.
points: Friendship patterns vary across cultures and individuals.
Possessions do not determine everyone’s popularity.
Children negotiate family and community expectations.
Safety and inclusion shape opportunities.
topics.example: A class develops a fair way to include a new student in a game.

topics.title: Adolescent identity and relationships
topics.core: Privacy, peer affiliation, body awareness and future planning become prominent. Conflict or risk is not inevitable, and supportive family relationships remain relevant.
points: Media messages can affect self-presentation.
Autonomy and connection can coexist.
Later planning may become more realistic.
Do not assume one universal sequence of friendship or gender-group patterns.
topics.example: A teenager negotiates privacy while agreeing on a communication plan with caregivers.

topics.title: Adaptive assessment
topics.core: The Vineland family of instruments evaluates adaptive functioning through domains such as communication, daily living and socialization, with motor content depending on edition and form.
points: Use the appropriate standardized version.
Reports reflect opportunities and setting.
Scores need qualified interpretation.
Screening, assessment and diagnosis are different activities.
topics.example: A child’s daily-living profile can reveal support needs that are not captured by an academic test.

milestones.text: Face regard, responsiveness and social smiling support interaction.
Imitation, gestures, shared games and familiar-person preferences become more evident.
Participating in feeding and dressing, communicating needs and seeking help.
Peer play, turn-taking, simple rules and increasing self-care with support.
Friendship, belonging, teachers, prosocial behavior and community expectations broaden participation.
Privacy, identity, peers and future planning coexist with continuing relationships and support needs.

questions.question: What does adaptive functioning concern?
questions.explanation: Adaptive functioning includes daily living and communication used in context. Feeding or dressing with appropriate support are examples.

questions.question: Which example is prosocial behavior?
options: Ignoring a request for help every time
Helping a peer pick up dropped materials
Taking a toy without regard for others
questions.explanation: Prosocial behavior benefits another person. Helping, sharing and comforting are common examples, although ability and context vary.

questions.question: What is a sensible approach to toilet learning?
options: Consider readiness, support and individual variation
Assume one fixed age fits every child
Require complete night dryness by the second birthday
questions.explanation: Toileting develops with readiness and practice; night dryness can follow a different course. A rigid birthday rule can mislead.

questions.question: Why do peer relationships matter in middle childhood?
options: They provide opportunities for cooperation and belonging
questions.explanation: Friendships offer practice in negotiation, empathy and group participation. Family and adult relationships remain important.

questions.question: Which response supports turn-taking?
options: Model it and practise with manageable waits
Label every difficulty as bad character
questions.explanation: Short, supported turns provide practice. The adult can say “your turn, then mine” and gradually increase waiting.

questions.question: What should a standardized adaptive assessment use?
options: The appropriate edition and trained interpretation
A score detached from cultural context
One skill as the total adaptive profile
A homemade copy treated as an official score
questions.explanation: Tools such as Vineland have specific editions and procedures. A valid interpretation considers the person's context and multiple domains.

questions.question: Which statement about adolescent development is most appropriate?
options: Privacy is proof of a disorder
Every adolescent has the same priorities
Peers erase the importance of caregivers
Growing independence can coexist with a need for support
questions.explanation: Adolescents negotiate identity, privacy and relationships. Support can evolve while allowing greater responsibility.

questions.question: Why is cultural context important in self-care assessment?
options: It means functional abilities never matter
Expectations and opportunities to practise differ
It allows one universal routine for every household
questions.explanation: Daily tasks are taught and valued differently across settings. Assessment should distinguish limited opportunity from difficulty performing a skill.

questions.question: What is the best way to interpret difficulty sharing at age three?
options: Consider emerging regulation, context and support needs
Assume sharing should always be perfect
questions.explanation: Sharing draws on language, inhibition and perspective-taking, which are still developing. Adults can model and scaffold it.

questions.question: Which observation best reflects social participation?
options: The presence of a newborn grasp reflex
The eruption of a permanent molar
Joining a group activity and responding to peers
questions.explanation: Participation concerns involvement in meaningful activities with others. It depends on both the child's skills and the environment's support.

clarifications.title: Everyday skills vary
clarifications.text: Toileting, especially night dryness, is not universally complete at age two. Sharing is still developing in preschool. Peer patterns are not fixed by sex. Adaptive tools must be interpreted using the correct edition, procedures and cultural context.
